segments.vo: A wave of molasses once killed twenty-one people. This really happened.
January fifteenth, nineteen nineteen. Around twelve thirty in the afternoon.
In Boston's North End, near the harbor, stood a giant steel tank.
It held two point three million gallons of molasses.
segments.cap: It held 2.3 million gallons of molasses.

segments.vo: It was meant to be turned into industrial alcohol.
And it leaked so badly that it was painted brown to hide the drips.
A wave of molasses up to twenty-five feet high tore through the streets at an estimated thirty-five miles an hour.
segments.cap: A wave up to 25 feet high tore through the streets at an estimated 35 mph.

segments.vo: It trapped people and horses. Twenty-one people died, and about one hundred fifty were injured.
segments.cap: It trapped people and horses. 21 people died, and about 150 were injured.

segments.vo: Rescuers waded through the sticky mess for days, searching for survivors.

events.label: Crews hose the streets with seawater
The harbor finally stops running brown

segments.vo: Cleanup took weeks, and the harbor stayed brown until summer.
Residents sued, and after three years of hearings, the owner paid six hundred twenty-eight thousand dollars.
segments.cap: Residents sued, and after three years of hearings, the owner paid $628,000.

segments.vo: For decades, locals claimed the neighborhood still smelled of molasses on hot summer days.
The disaster changed building laws, requiring licensed architects and engineers to oversee projects like this.
